lesson: Fade inflated scoring/margin (team-total overs, -1.5 handicaps, match overs) when a favorite projects as a CONTROL/territorial team rather than a clear chance-creator — i.e., possession dominance without elite finishing volume, a missing main creative/transition threat, a rotated or below-full-strength attacking XI, or a disciplined low-threat underdog that caps the ceiling. The market often overprices reputation and 'control guarantees goals.' This makes team-goal unders, match unders, anti-handicap, and small draw exposure correlated value.

Do NOT fade a strong favorite's multi-goal win when the matchup genuinely points to sustained pressure AND elite finishing — i.e., midfield control PLUS proven conversion options against a weak/overmatched opponent. 'Not an overwhelming favorite' or squad-quality skepticism alone is insufficient to oppose the handicap or over; respect blowout tail risk in extreme mismatches where early goals or defensive collapse cascade into large margins.

Recognize that anti-scoring positions (opposing 2+ team goals, opposing the handicap, opposing match overs) are HIGHLY CORRELATED — they win and lose together. When your strongest edges all align on a low-scoring thesis it is reasonable to trust the stack, but size it as one concentrated bet, not as independent diversified edges, because a single early goal or collapse fails all of them simultaneously.

Before drawing tactical or performance lessons from a result, verify settlement and label integrity: confirm which side 'NO'/'No' refers to and whether a line was actually cleared. A bet that beat its line is not a model loss; mislabeled or misattributed settlements create false negative signals that corrupt future reasoning.

Watch out for betting “NO” on team over 1.5 goals when the edge is modest and the opponent may not suppress chance quality. A 53% position losing is normal variance, but future unders need stronger matchup/tempo support beyond price discrepancy.

Watch out for taking “NO” on a favorite’s 1.5 team-goals line when their XI is strong and they project to dominate territory/midfield. Price edge isn’t enough; require clear evidence of low tempo or defensive resilience before fading 2+ goals.

Watch out for translating a favorite’s territorial/control edge and opponent attacking absences into unders or “NO” on favorite scoring/handicap markets. When the mismatch points to one-way pressure, blowout risk can dominate even if the weaker side offers little going forward.

Watch out for fading a heavy favorite's scoring against weak opposition: betting NO on dominant teams covering handicaps or hitting goal totals invites losses when expected blowouts materialize. Reserve under/NO-goals bets for the total ceiling, not the favorite's margin or team-goal floor.

Watch out for fading goals when backing a strong attacking favorite: betting "under/no" on totals against a team with high shot volume and chance creation invites blow-ups. When your own analysis cites sustained pressure, don't lean on low-scoring outcomes.

Confirmed: Fading an inflated favourite's goal-scoring expectations pays off when the market overprices their attacking output—strong defensive sides and tactical underdogs can stifle even clear favourites. Backing the "under/no" on overhyped scorelines captures value across multiple goal lines simultaneously.

Watch out for fading goal totals when a dominant favourite faces a heavy underdog. Backing "unders" against elite attacking sides invites blowout risk; their territorial and technical superiority often converts into multiple goals, so don't overweight the chance of a low-scoring game.

Don't overweight a model's edge on team-total unders for stronger sides; quality favorites with high shot volume frequently exceed 1.5 goals, so betting against their scoring requires a larger margin than a thin 10% gap.

Watch out for backing UNDER on team goals when you already rate that team a clear favorite with superior attacking quality—a 57% model edge against your own thesis is a red flag. If you believe a side creates the better chances, lean toward their goals OVER, not under.

Watch out for fading a clear favourite's team-goal total when your own model only marginally supports the bet (52%). Backing the under on elite attacking sides at neutral venues offers thin edge and high variance—demand stronger conviction before betting against quality offenses.

Confirmed: In clear mismatches, fading inflated team-goal totals (e.g., over 3.5) pays off—dominant favorites often win comfortably without running up extreme scorelines, so the market overprices high-goal thresholds.

Watch out for fading a strong favorite's goal output against weak opposition; betting NO on team-goal overlines underestimates how lopsided talent mismatches can blow out. When a top side faces clearly inferior defenses, lean toward overs, not unders.

Confirmed: When the market overprices a favorite's scoring ceiling, fading inflated over/goal lines (backing the "NO") captures real value. Strong-but-not-overwhelming favorites on neutral fields often underdeliver on goals, so don't assume attacking talent automatically translates to high scorelines.

Confirmed: backing under team-goal lines for a favorite that's strong but not dominant—especially on neutral ground with key creators benched—can hold value when the model edge (57% vs 47%) is genuine. Low-scoring outputs from quality-but-not-clinical teams reward fading inflated overs.

Don't fade overs against a dominant favorite when the market prices high scoring—the model repeatedly underestimated goal totals by betting NO on overs. When a strong attacking team faces a weaker side, lean toward goals, not against them.

Watch out for systematically underestimating a strong favourite's scoring against a weak opponent. Betting "under" on goal totals (NO over X) failed across the board when the model overweighted competitiveness vs elite sides while ignoring blowout potential against minnows. Don't fade a clear favourite's goal output based on their performance against top teams.

lesson: Confirmed: When the model identifies a genuine edge over market price on a team-total under, backing it pays off—especially against favorites who can dominate possession yet fail to convert into multiple goals. Don't assume control equals goal volume.

Watch out for goal-total cutoffs near the actual scoreline: backing "under 2.5" lost while "under 3.5" won on a 3-goal game. When a match lands exactly on your threshold, small edges in model probability offer little real protection—favor under bets only when the cushion above expected goals is comfortable.

lesson: Watch out for backing "under team goals" on attacking sides fielding weakened XIs—even depleted lineups can convert against vulnerable defenses. A modest model edge over market (61% vs 50%) doesn't justify confidence when you're betting against a team's proven scoring upside.

Confirmed: When the model finds a large edge on an underdog scoring (BTTS/team over 0.5), back it—even dominant favorites concede, and markets often over-discount a weaker side's ability to find one goal.

Confirmed: Backing UNDER a strong favorite's team-goal total can offer value, since dominant sides often win by a single goal despite controlling play—class doesn't guarantee multiple goals. Favoring quality over scoring volume when the market overprices a blowout is sound.

Confirmed: Even heavy underdogs facing dominant favorites often manage at least one goal, so backing the weaker side to score (BTTS or team over 0.5) holds value when the market overprices a clean sheet. Talent gaps drive scorelines, not shutouts.

Watch out for backing overs in evenly-matched, defensively resilient mid-tier matchups; tight, cagey games often settle low-scoring (here 1-1). An individual-talent "ceiling" argument doesn't override the base rate when both sides prioritize resilience.

Confirmed: In tight matchups between two strong, full-strength sides, backing a team to stay UNDER its goal line offers value—elite defenses and cagey play suppress scoring, so favor unders when quality is balanced and motivation high.

lesson: Watch out for backing UNDER on a team's goals in must-win knockout scenarios; defensive resilience often gives way to attacking urgency, and a model edge over a coin-flip market price isn't enough margin to justify fading a motivated favorite's scoring.

Confirmed: When an elite, deep squad faces a clear minnow, backing goal-scoring overs at prices below model probability pays off—class gaps in attacking output are persistently underpriced by markets.

Confirmed: When two evenly-matched, high-volume attacking sides meet and the market underprices goals, backing overs across multiple thresholds pays off. Trust shot-volume signals to identify systematically underpriced over markets.

Confirmed: When a talent-laden favorite shows high shot volume, backing modest over lines (1.5, 2.5) with positive edge pays off—but don't stretch the same thesis to higher lines (3.5+), where goal totals rarely climb that far. Scale exposure down as the line rises.

Confirmed: Backing the under on a heavy favorite's team goals—and value on a disciplined underdog advancing—pays off when the favorite faces a low-block defense that suppresses clear chances. Fade inflated scoreline expectations when one side concedes possession but limits quality shots.

Watch out for backing a "value" underdog purely on perceived evenness when the opponent has clearly superior attacking talent; concentrated individual quality (a top striker plus creators) often decides tight knockout matches. Don't overrate model edges that contradict your own read on firepower.

Watch out for backing big underdogs purely on a model-vs-market edge: when an elite, full-strength favorite faces a clear gap in quality, the market's low price often reflects reality. A perceived 9% edge isn't worth chasing if the core thesis still has the favorite winning comfortably.

Watch out for overriding market prices with large model edges in cagey knockout matches; a 12-point gap on a coin-flip advancement bet often reflects information you're missing, not value. Don't discount an opponent's strong form just because their clean sheets came against "modest" attacks.

Confirmed: Backing an underdog to score against a favorite with shaky defensive/conversion track record pays off when the market underprices their goal chances. When model edge is 10%+ on "team to score" or BTTS at low prices, the value is real.

lesson: Watch out for backing an underdog's goal-scoring markets when your own analysis concludes the opponent is clearly superior — if the model rates the other side's XI and form as dominant, don't simultaneously assign large edges to the weaker team scoring. Reconcile the qualitative read with the probabilities; a 70% "over 0.5 goals" for the outclassed side was likely overconfident, not just variance.

Watch out for backing underdogs against elite sides purely because the market price looks low — a 26% model vs 14% market edge is meaningless if the model overweights "anything can happen" variance against a dominant, fully-fit favorite with an unbeaten record and clean defensive sheet. When the favorite's only flaw is finishing luck, that flaw tends to regress in their favor, not the underdog's.

Watch out for betting against a stronger team's goal totals when your own reasoning acknowledges their dominance — full-strength elite attacks controlling possession routinely clear 1.5 team goals. A perceived price edge shouldn't override the fundamental mismatch; the market's higher probability on favorites scoring twice often reflects real attacking quality. A single loss like this is also within normal variance.

Watch out for backing overs when one side is a dominant, controlled favorite in tournament football: superior teams often win efficiently (2-0) without pushing for extra goals, keeping totals under. A 10-point edge on overs built mostly on team-quality signals, rather than tempo/chance-creation metrics for both sides, is fragile — though a single loss like this is also within normal variance.

Watch out for translating shot-volume dominance and star attacker presence into team-total-goals overs at premium prices — a single goal remains the modal outcome for even strong attacks against organized opposition. A one-goal result here is normal variance, but demand a bigger edge before backing team overs 1.5 against the market.

Confirmed: markets systematically overprice goal totals for elite favorites against proven defensive underdogs — fading team-goal overs (unders) was profitable both times. But don't extend that edge to the underdog actually advancing: a stubborn defense caps the scoreline without flipping the result. Bet the low-scoring angle, not the upset.

Watch out for betting against a clearly stronger side "at a price" — the model acknowledged Morocco's superiority in every writeup, yet still faded them on the advance and team-goals markets purely because the market number looked beatable. When your own reasoning identifies one team as materially better, don't let a perceived edge justify contrarian bets on the weaker side or on low-scoring outcomes against them.

Watch out for betting "value" on longshot upsets against elite teams solely because the market price looks low. When a heavy favorite has confirmed strength, form, and full squad, a 8-9% market price on the underdog is often accurate — inflating it to 18-19% doubles a small edge into a systematic overpricing of chaos. Demand concrete upset catalysts, not just base-rate uncertainty.

Watch out for backing high team-goal totals purely off strong underlying stats (shots, possession) — favorites often underperform their xG against organized, counterattacking opponents. A single loss at 35% probability is normal variance, but demanding 3+ goals from one team is a high bar; require evidence of finishing quality and weak opposing defense, not just volume metrics.

The favorite-side edge held but the underdog's scoring output didn't: backing the stronger team to advance can be correct even when they concede more than expected. Don't couple "team A wins" with "team B stays quiet"—a superior side can win shootout-style games. Treat unders on the underdog's goals as a separate, riskier bet, not a byproduct of the winner call.

Confirmed: in high-stakes matches between two elite full-strength sides, unders and "no" goal markets are often underpriced — the public overweights star attacking talent while cautious tactics and strong defenses suppress scoring. When one team has elite defensive numbers (e.g., zero conceded in the tournament), fading goals across correlated low-scoring markets can offer consistent edge.

Confirmed: fading a weaker team's goal totals based on the stronger side's chance-creation dominance is sound, but bet the moderate line (under 1.5) rather than the extreme one (clean sheet). Even dominated underdogs often snag a single goal, so shutout bets carry thin margins; results here were consistent with that expected variance.

Mixed but consistent with the model's own logic: underdogs with elite attackers (Salah-type) can score against stronger sides without seriously threatening to advance. Prefer backing underdog goals/team totals over underdog advancement when the edge comes from attacking talent rather than overall squad quality. The advancement loss at 26% is normal variance, not a model error.

Watch out for large model edges (73% vs 54%) on "advances" markets that hinge on extra time and penalties — shootouts are near coin-flips regardless of team quality, so cap your true probability closer to the market. A 0-0 draw shows how easily perceived superiority evaporates into a lottery; treat this loss as expected variance, but shade advancement probabilities toward 50-60% when penalties are plausible.

Watch out for backing underdogs purely on a perceived market mispricing when your own reasoning highlights the favorite's dominance across every fundamental (form, squad strength, attack quality). A modest model edge (32% vs 23%) on a defensive underdog is fragile; a single loss here is normal variance, but ensure the edge isn't just narrative-driven optimism about resilient defenses.

Confirmed: in elite-vs-elite matchups, don't assume both defenses get breached just because both attacks are strong — top sides often produce lopsided or clean-sheet results. When the model sees a near coin-flip but the market prices BTTS-No cheaply, that edge is worth taking. Single-bet sample, though — treat as consistent with normal variance.

Confirmed: in elite-vs-elite matchups, especially with a recent head-to-head goalless result, low-scoring outcomes (No BTTS, unders) are often underpriced by markets that default to expecting goals from strong attacks. Recent direct-matchup evidence between the same sides is a strong signal worth backing when it diverges from market price.
